author: Olivia Kasmin
title: Bureaucracy in the Revolutionary War Era; The Very Human Burden of Applying for a Pension
description: This project explores pension data from the Revolution Crossroads - NARA Revolutionary War Pension Files collection. It provides historical context for the collection and examines the distribution of applications attributed to each category (survivors, widows, rejected, bounty land warrant, old war, and national archives accession). I also extracted data from the text using a lightweight LLM model to collect the dollar amount awarded to the recipient as well as other related fields, such as where the pension was issued and which congressional act it corresponds to. This analysis is presented through an interactive  interface that allows users to select a year, applicant type and location. A matching record is fetched and the scan is displayed for users to see a real example of this case.

author: Maggie Navracruz
title: America's Stamp Collection
subtitle: Stamps as revolutionary marks
description: This project explores how we can trace a path through history using the National Postal Museum's collection of stamps and letters - from the first stamp as part of The Stamp Act of 1765 to where they begin to live more permanently in America's modern day postal system and culture. Categorized by decade from 1760 to 1890, themes, colors, materials, and imagery are extracted and supplemented with historical context to explore how their history laid the foundation for stamps to become a symbol of resistance, revolutionary spirit, and independence.

author: Lara Yeyati Preiss
title: The Ordinaries
subtitle: Artifacts of daily use
description: This project examines the American Revolutionary period by shifting attention from monuments and heroes to the material traces of everyday life. The site opens with a scrollytelling sequence introducing selected objects and the habits and roles tied to them, revealing how daily routines offer glimpses of what once constituted a life. Objects are then arranged in a zoomable treemap—explorable by action family or material—with a details panel linking directly to the Smithsonian collection.

author: Saehun Kim
title: Paper Trail
subtitle: Laguage patterns in revolutionary documents
description: The project maps the language of over 450 revolutionary-era documents(1770-1810) from the Smithsonian Revolutionary Crossroads collection. By classifying each document by topic - Military, Society, Political, Religion, and Business - and analyzing keyword frequencies, it visualizes how words circulated across different contexts rather than how they changed over time. The interface allows users to filter and explore recurring terms, revealing linguistic networks in that era.

author: Neven Armanios-Rodriguez
title: Silhouette Art of Early America
subtitle: Silhouette art by William Bache
description: Silhouette Art of Early America is a data visualization inspired by the work of William Bache. It explores approximately 1830 of his silhouettes. The sitters include unidentified as well as named men, women and children that can be filtered. A technique used to create these silhouettes involved carefully tracing a person's profile using a device called a physiognotrace. The outlines and tracing of these profiles is visualized in this project. Any combination of silhouettes can be selected and explored at a time.

author: Nichos Molnar
title: Faces of the Revolution
subtitle: Tracking the changing faces of early America
description: The Revolutionary Crossroads supercollection has several pieces that contain 'sitters'. While the media type can change - from oil paintings, to coins, to graphic prints - these items all depict someone. Some sitters are depicted several times throughout the collection, most notably George Washington and other 'founding fathers' of the American Revolution. How did the depiction of these sitters change over the course of their lives, as the aged, participated in important early American historical events, and eventually passed away? Using data from the Revolutionary Crossroads dataset (linked above), I found sitters who were depicted in multiple (>10) objects, visually cropped their faces, and arranged them on an annotated timeline. By highlighting key dates, I hope viewers can see how historical events can influence the type and frequency of depiction for these important people.

author: Sofia Molina
title: Art of Scale
subtitle: Tracing size, form, and scale across Revolutionary-era art
description: Art of Scale is a project that explores the physical dimensions and visual impact of artworks from The Revolutionary Era Art Collections across different historical decades. It analyzes how the physical size of the art, which includes 18th-century miniatures and larger canvases, has changed or remained consistent over time, using real dimensions to visually illustrate these scale differences for the entire dataset of paintings and miniatures.

author: Derin Savasan
title: Remember Me
subtitle: Who gets framed, and who gets forgotten
description: Remember Me looks at portraits from the American Revolution and asks a basic question: who actually made it into the frame? I scraped data from the National Portrait Gallery and built a set of interactives (filters, memory game) that let you see the gaps for yourself. Men everywhere. Women barely visible. A handful of artists shaping what the “founders” even look like. It's history told through portraits, but the absences say more than the faces. This isn't about patriotism. It's about who gets remembered, and who gets edited out.

author: LuisPablo Padres
title: America Through The Journalist Glass
subtitle: Analyzing the distribution of information through journalistic publications throughout Revolutionary America
description: This project follows a database of journalistic issues from a variety of news publications from multiple states in Revolutionary America. The purpose of the project is to view this time in our country thorugh a journalisitc perspective. What states were pushing out the most information? What was the information? What years were the most information codensed? All these questions are meant to push the user into an inmersive experience where they can view the real-time information that was being shared at the time.
